# Conti Ransomware Leaks and Public Attribution Record

## Executive Summary

Public sources describe Conti as a large, commercially organized ransomware-as-a-service (RaaS) operation that combined internally developed malware, external affiliates, initial-access brokers, negotiation personnel, and specialized technical staff. Its operational model used double extortion: operators stole victim data, encrypted systems, demanded payment, and threatened to publish or sell the stolen material if victims refused to pay. The available record presents Conti as more than a malware strain; it describes an enterprise-like criminal organization that divided labor, recruited personnel, purchased tools and access, and continuously tested and improved its ransomware. ([CIS, n.d.](https://www.cisecurity.org/insights/blog/the-conti-leaks-a-case-of-cybercrimes-commercialization)) [S3]

The February–March 2022 ContiLeaks disclosures materially expanded public understanding of that organization. Rapid7 reported that the leaked material included approximately 14 megabytes of chat logs across 393 JSON files, screenshots of tools and control panels, discussions of exploits and malware design, usernames and passwords, and information allegedly related to command-and-control and storage servers. Rapid7 did not access the exposed remote systems and advised others not to do so. ([Rapid7, 2022](https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/2022/03/01/conti-ransomware-group-internal-chats-leaked-over-russia-ukraine-conflict/)) [S2]

The leaks also revealed an internal division of labor. CIS, summarizing KrebsOnSecurity’s analysis and an MS-ISAC perspective, described “Coders,” “Testers,” “Administrators,” “Reverse Engineers,” and “Penetration Testers/Hackers,” with spamming functions contracted externally. CIS reported that an insider estimated the group employed more than 60 people in July 2021, although staffing fluctuated. ([CIS, n.d.](https://www.cisecurity.org/insights/blog/the-conti-leaks-a-case-of-cybercrimes-commercialization)) [S3]

Law-enforcement and government records provide a separate attribution layer. The U.S. Department of State’s Rewards for Justice program identifies the online aliases “Target,” “Reshaev,” “Professor,” “Tramp,” and “Dandis” as malicious cyber actors believed to be linked to Conti and Wizard Spider. It offers a reward of up to $10 million for information leading to the identification or location of persons acting at the direction or control of a foreign government in malicious cyber activity against U.S. critical infrastructure. ([Rewards for Justice, n.d.](https://rewardsforjustice.net/rewards/conti/)) [S1]

The U.S. Department of Justice separately identifies Maksim Galochkin, Maksim Rudenskiy, Mikhail Tsarev, Andrey Zhuykov, and Oleksii Lytvynenko as defendants in Conti-related federal cases. The DOJ page states that the first four were charged with conspiracy to violate the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act and conspiracy to commit wire fraud, while Lytvynenko was charged with conspiracy to deploy Conti and later pleaded guilty to conspiracy to commit wire fraud. The records supplied do not establish that any of these defendants is one of the five aliases listed by Rewards for Justice. ([U.S. Department of Justice, 2026](https://www.justice.gov/usao-mdtn/conti-ransomware-2)) [S4]

Overall, the strongest evidence supports a conclusion that Conti was a structured, scalable RaaS enterprise whose internal communications corroborated a corporate-style operating model. The public attribution record links multiple aliases and named defendants to Conti-related activity, but it does not, in the supplied sources, establish a one-to-one identity mapping between those aliases and defendants.

## Source Set and Evidentiary Weight

For purposes of this report, the supplied sources are assigned the following identifiers:

| ID | Source | Evidentiary character |
|---|---|---|
| S1 | Rewards for Justice, “Conti” | Official U.S. government attribution and reward notice |
| S2 | Rapid7, “Conti Ransomware Group Internal Chats Leaked Over Russia-Ukraine Conflict” | Technical analysis of leaked material and operational behavior |
| S3 | Center for Internet Security, “The Conti Leaks: A Case of Cybercrime’s Commercialization” | Cybersecurity-sector synthesis of the leaks and RaaS structure |
| S4 | U.S. Department of Justice, Middle District of Tennessee, “Conti Ransomware” | Official criminal-case and defendant record |

S1 and S4 carry the greatest weight for formal government attribution and legal status. S2 and S3 are valuable for reconstructing internal organization and technical operations, but their descriptions of leaked material are not equivalent to judicial findings. The DOJ page expressly states that defendants are presumed innocent until proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt. ([U.S. Department of Justice, 2026](https://www.justice.gov/usao-mdtn/conti-ransomware-2)) [S4]

## How Public Sources Describe Conti’s RaaS Model

### Commercialization and division of labor

The sources consistently describe Conti as a RaaS operation. In the RaaS model, a core group develops and maintains ransomware while affiliates conduct or support intrusions. CIS explains that affiliates may share ransom proceeds with developers, and that initial-access brokers can sell established access to victim environments. This division allows the central operator to scale attacks without personally conducting every intrusion. ([CIS, n.d.](https://www.cisecurity.org/insights/blog/the-conti-leaks-a-case-of-cybercrimes-commercialization)) [S3]

This model is important because it separates several functions that would otherwise be performed by a single criminal team. Developers can focus on malware engineering, affiliates can focus on intrusion and deployment, and brokers can supply access. CIS’s account therefore characterizes Conti’s criminal activity as an enterprise with specialized production, distribution, and revenue functions rather than as a loose collection of individuals. ([CIS, n.d.](https://www.cisecurity.org/insights/blog/the-conti-leaks-a-case-of-cybercrimes-commercialization)) [S3]

Rewards for Justice uses similar terminology, describing Conti as “Russian government-linked” and identifying it also as Wizard Spider. The government notice says Conti used Conti ransomware-as-a-service and associated the operation with TrickBot, IcedID, Cobalt Strike, and ZLoader. The source presents these relationships as government assessments or associations, not as a complete criminal adjudication of every person or tool named. ([Rewards for Justice, n.d.](https://rewardsforjustice.net/rewards/conti/)) [S1]

### Double extortion and victim pressure

The public record describes Conti’s core extortion process as involving both encryption and data theft. Operators allegedly stole files and encrypted servers and workstations, then directed victims to an online portal for ransom negotiations. If victims did not pay, the stolen data could be published or sold through infrastructure controlled by the operators. ([Rewards for Justice, n.d.](https://rewardsforjustice.net/rewards/conti/)) [S1]

CIS similarly characterizes Conti as a RaaS operation using double extortion. The term refers to the combined threat of loss of access through encryption and disclosure of stolen data. This approach increases pressure on victims because restoring backups alone may not prevent confidentiality harms, regulatory exposure, or reputational damage. ([CIS, n.d.](https://www.cisecurity.org/insights/blog/the-conti-leaks-a-case-of-cybercrimes-commercialization)) [S3]

### Scale and victimology

Rewards for Justice states that Conti was first detected in 2019 and had been used in more than 1,000 ransomware operations targeting U.S. and international critical infrastructure. The same notice states that more than 400 organizations worldwide were victimized, including more than 290 in the United States, and identifies law-enforcement agencies, emergency medical services, 9-1-1 dispatch centers, municipalities, healthcare organizations, and first-responder networks among the affected sectors. ([Rewards for Justice, n.d.](https://rewardsforjustice.net/rewards/conti/)) [S1]

The DOJ’s Middle District of Tennessee page gives a different aggregate figure, stating that Conti ransomware affected more than 900 businesses, nonprofits, governments, and other victims in the United States and around the world. The figures are not necessarily irreconcilable: “more than 1,000 ransomware operations” and “more than 900 victims” could refer to different counting methods, time periods, or categories. However, the supplied sources do not explain the methodology behind either figure. The discrepancy should therefore be reported rather than silently resolved. ([U.S. Department of Justice, 2026](https://www.justice.gov/usao-mdtn/conti-ransomware-2); [Rewards for Justice, n.d.](https://rewardsforjustice.net/rewards/conti/)) [S1] [S4]

## What the Leaks Revealed About Conti’s Internal Structure

### The leak and its provenance

Rapid7 reported that a Twitter account identified as @ContiLeaks released a large archive of internal Conti communications beginning on February 27, 2022. The first archive, named `1.tgz`, reportedly contained 14 megabytes of chat logs distributed across 393 JSON files. Some messages were encrypted and unreadable, meaning the resulting picture was incomplete. Additional files and pro-Ukraine messages followed on February 28 and March 1. ([Rapid7, 2022](https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/2022/03/01/conti-ransomware-group-internal-chats-leaked-over-russia-ukraine-conflict/)) [S2]

The leak’s completeness and authenticity cannot be treated as absolute based only on the supplied sources. Rapid7 stated that some communications were encrypted and that the scale of the material suggested the leaker was likely either a senior member or a coalition of disgruntled affiliates. “Likely” is an analytical assessment, not a proven identification of the leaker. ([Rapid7, 2022](https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/2022/03/01/conti-ransomware-group-internal-chats-leaked-over-russia-ukraine-conflict/)) [S2]

### Corporate-style staffing

CIS reports that the leaked communications showed distinct operational roles. “Coders” wrote malicious code and integrated technologies; “Testers” evaluated how ransomware performed against security products; “Administrators,” “Reverse Engineers,” and “Penetration Testers/Hackers” performed other internal functions. Spamming was reportedly contracted outside the organization. Departments had their own budgets, while units could borrow from one another. ([CIS, n.d.](https://www.cisecurity.org/insights/blog/the-conti-leaks-a-case-of-cybercrimes-commercialization)) [S3]

CIS also reports an insider estimate of more than 60 employees in July 2021, mostly coders and testers. Staffing was not static, and personnel could be dismissed following security breaches. This evidence supports the conclusion that Conti had managerial and human-resources characteristics commonly associated with a business, while not implying that it was a legally registered or legitimate corporation. ([CIS, n.d.](https://www.cisecurity.org/insights/blog/the-conti-leaks-a-case-of-cybercrimes-commercialization)) [S3]

Rapid7’s description reinforces this interpretation. The chats reportedly included interviews, coding exercises hosted on public repositories, salary negotiations, out-of-office messages, product discussions, and service payments. These details are especially significant because they show ordinary administrative processes embedded within a criminal operation. ([Rapid7, 2022](https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/2022/03/01/conti-ransomware-group-internal-chats-leaked-over-russia-ukraine-conflict/)) [S2]

### Product development and testing

The leaks reportedly showed Conti treating ransomware as a product requiring continuous engineering and quality assurance. Rapid7 described discussions about adding features, encrypting very large files, and obtaining demonstrations of endpoint-detection software so that malware could be adjusted to avoid detection. ([Rapid7, 2022](https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/2022/03/01/conti-ransomware-group-internal-chats-leaked-over-russia-ukraine-conflict/)) [S2]

CIS reported several specific investments identified through analysis of the leaks: approximately $60,000 for a valid Cobalt Strike license, several thousand dollars per month for security and antivirus software used in testing, and a July 2021 decision to focus reverse engineering on Windows 11. These details support the assessment that Conti reinvested revenue into tools, testing, and platform compatibility. ([CIS, n.d.](https://www.cisecurity.org/insights/blog/the-conti-leaks-a-case-of-cybercrimes-commercialization)) [S3]

### Access, phishing, and operational infrastructure

Rapid7 reported that Conti commonly used phishing to establish an initial presence on target networks. The leaked materials allegedly included phishing templates, discussions of malicious-document providers, logistics for delivering ransomware while avoiding dynamic analysis, screenshots of a control panel, and information about compromised hosts and their operating systems, antivirus products, user rights, and asset details. ([Rapid7, 2022](https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/2022/03/01/conti-ransomware-group-internal-chats-leaked-over-russia-ukraine-conflict/)) [S2]

Rapid7 also listed vulnerabilities associated with Conti activity, including MS17-010-related vulnerabilities, ZeroLogon, PrintNightmare, Log4Shell, and ProxyShell/ProxyLogon vulnerabilities. The list demonstrates the breadth of publicly discussed technical exposure associated with Conti, but it does not prove that every listed vulnerability was used in every intrusion. ([Rapid7, 2022](https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/2022/03/01/conti-ransomware-group-internal-chats-leaked-over-russia-ukraine-conflict/)) [S2]

## Political Context and Operational Continuity

The leak occurred after Conti operators publicly expressed support for the Russian government following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. Rapid7 reported that internal disagreement followed, with some members supporting Ukraine. Two days later, Conti revised its public position, saying it condemned the war and would retaliate only if Russian critical infrastructure were targeted. ([Rapid7, 2022](https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/2022/03/01/conti-ransomware-group-internal-chats-leaked-over-russia-ukraine-conflict/)) [S2]

Rewards for Justice describes Conti as Russian government-linked and states that operators threatened infrastructure in countries perceived to be conducting cyberattacks or war against the Russian government. This is a formal U.S. government characterization, but the supplied page does not provide a detailed evidentiary explanation for the government-linkage assessment. It should therefore be presented as an official assessment rather than as an independently proven fact. ([Rewards for Justice, n.d.](https://rewardsforjustice.net/rewards/conti/)) [S1]

Rapid7 initially assessed that Conti remained active despite the leak and reported a resumption of normal operations by March 9, 2022. CIS later reported that the larger Conti platform shut down and rebranded into smaller units in May 2022, followed approximately a month later by the shutdown of leak and negotiation infrastructure. These statements can be reconciled as describing different stages: short-term operational recovery after the leak followed by later dismantling or fragmentation. ([Rapid7, 2022](https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/2022/03/01/conti-ransomware-group-internal-chats-leaked-over-russia-ukraine-conflict/); [CIS, n.d.](https://www.cisecurity.org/insights/blog/the-conti-leaks-a-case-of-cybercrimes-commercialization)) [S2] [S3]

## Law-Enforcement and Government Attribution Record

### Rewards for Justice aliases

S1 identifies five online aliases—“Target,” “Reshaev,” “Professor,” “Tramp,” and “Dandis”—as malicious cyber actors believed to be linked to Conti. It also associates them with Russia, Conti, Wizard Spider, and applications or tools including Conti ransomware-as-a-service, TrickBot, IcedID, Cobalt Strike, and ZLoader. ([Rewards for Justice, n.d.](https://rewardsforjustice.net/rewards/conti/)) [S1]

The notice offers up to $10 million for information leading to the identification or location of any person who, while acting at the direction or under the control of a foreign government, participates in malicious cyber activity against U.S. critical infrastructure in violation of the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act. The reward language is conditional and does not itself constitute a criminal conviction or establish that every listed alias corresponds to a publicly identified individual. ([Rewards for Justice, n.d.](https://rewardsforjustice.net/rewards/conti/)) [S1]

### DOJ defendants and procedural status

The DOJ page identifies two case numbers. Case 3:23-CR-00092 names Maksim Galochkin, Maksim Rudenskiy, Mikhail Tsarev, and Andrey Zhuykov. The page states that they were charged with conspiracy to violate the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act and conspiracy to commit wire fraud. Case 3:23-CR-00088 concerns Oleksii Lytvynenko, whom the page describes as charged with conspiracy to deploy Conti. ([U.S. Department of Justice, 2026](https://www.justice.gov/usao-mdtn/conti-ransomware-2)) [S4]

The same DOJ record states that Lytvynenko entered a guilty plea to Count 2, conspiracy to commit wire fraud, on June 10, 2026, and was scheduled for sentencing on September 10, 2026. As of the supplied page, the four other defendants remain described in charging language, and the DOJ expressly preserves the presumption of innocence. ([U.S. Department of Justice, 2026](https://www.justice.gov/usao-mdtn/conti-ransomware-2)) [S4]

### What the record does not establish

The supplied materials do not identify the real-world persons behind “Target,” “Reshaev,” “Professor,” “Tramp,” or “Dandis.” They also do not state that Galochkin, Rudenskiy, Tsarev, Zhuykov, or Lytvynenko used any of those aliases. Accordingly, a report that equates a particular alias with a particular defendant would exceed the evidence.

Likewise, the sources establish association among Conti, Wizard Spider, and certain malware or tools, but they do not provide a complete organizational chart, a definitive list of affiliates, or a comprehensive identity map. The proper conclusion is that the public record contains overlapping attribution layers—government assessments, technical reporting, leaked communications, and criminal charging records—but those layers should not be merged beyond what the sources expressly support.

## Contradictions and Uncertainty

| Issue | Evidence | Assessment |
|---|---|---|
| Scale of activity | S1 reports more than 1,000 operations and more than 400 organizations; S4 reports more than 900 victims | Different counting methods or populations may explain the difference; the sources do not resolve it. |
| Operational status after the leak | S2 reports resumed normal operations by March 9, 2022; S3 reports later shutdown and fragmentation in 2022 | Most consistent with short-term recovery followed by later dissolution or reorganization. |
| Government linkage | S1 calls Conti Russian government-linked; S2 reports a chat indicating alleged FSB interest and involvement in funding | Both are assessments or reported communications; the supplied evidence does not independently prove command-and-control relationships. |
| Alias-to-defendant identity | S1 lists aliases; S4 lists named defendants | No supplied source maps the aliases to the defendants. |

## Conclusion

The evidence supports a concrete conclusion: Conti was publicly documented as a sophisticated, commercially organized RaaS operation that scaled ransomware through specialization, affiliate relationships, purchased access, technical testing, and double extortion. The ContiLeaks disclosures were particularly important because they exposed the organization’s internal business processes—recruitment, salaries, budgets, departmental roles, product development, security testing, and operational logistics. ([Rapid7, 2022](https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/2022/03/01/conti-ransomware-group-internal-chats-leaked-over-russia-ukraine-conflict/); [CIS, n.d.](https://www.cisecurity.org/insights/blog/the-conti-leaks-a-case-of-cybercrimes-commercialization)) [S2] [S3]

The attribution record is substantial but bounded. Rewards for Justice publicly associates five aliases with Conti-linked malicious cyber activity and offers a reward for identifying qualifying actors. DOJ records establish Conti-related federal prosecutions involving five named defendants and document a guilty plea by Oleksii Lytvynenko. However, the supplied sources do not prove that the aliases and defendants are the same people. The most defensible assessment is therefore that public sources establish a network of Conti-related aliases, organizations, malware, alleged activity, and legal proceedings, while leaving important individual identity relationships unresolved. ([Rewards for Justice, n.d.](https://rewardsforjustice.net/rewards/conti/); [U.S. Department of Justice, 2026](https://www.justice.gov/usao-mdtn/conti-ransomware-2)) [S1] [S4]

Malicious cyber actors known by their online aliases of “Target,” “Reshaev,” “Professor,” “Tramp,” and “Dandis” are believed to be linked to the Conti ransomware group. Conti (also known as Wizard Spider), is a Russian government-linked ransomware-as-a-service (RaaS) group that has targeted U.S. and Western critical infrastructure. After Russian military forces invaded neighboring Ukraine in February 2022, Conti ransomware operators pledged support to the Russian government and threatened critical infrastructure organizations of countries perceived to carry out cyberattacks or war against the Russian government. First detected in 2019, Conti ransomware has been used to conduct more than 1,000 ransomware operations targeting U.S. and international critical infrastructure, such as law enforcement agencies, emergency medical services, 9-1-1 dispatch centers, and municipalities. These healthcare and first responder networks are among the more than 400 organizations worldwide victimized by Conti, over 290 of which are located in the United States. Conti operators typically steal victims’ files and encrypt the servers and workstations in an effort to force a ransom payment from the victim. The ransom letter instructs victims to contact the actors through an online portal to complete the transaction. If the ransom is not paid, the stolen data is sold or published to a public site controlled by the Conti actors. Ransom amounts vary widely, with some ransom demands being as high as $25 million. On February 27, Twitter user @ContiLeaks released a trove of chat logs from the ransomware group, Conti – a sophisticated ransomware group whose manual was publicly leaked last year . Ahead of the chat log disclosures, Conti pledged their support for the Russian Government following the Russian invasion of Ukraine. However, a number of members sided with Ukraine, causing strife within the organization. Two days later, Conti posted a second message revising their statement to condemn the war and to strike back only if Russian critical infrastructure is targeted. At the time of the leak, a file titled `1.tgz` was released on the “AnonFiles” website, containing 14 megabytes of chat logs across 393 JSON files. However, some of the messages were encrypted and could not be read, so the information provided is necessarily incomplete. The remaining files contained internal Conti communications, screenshots of tools, and discussions of their exploits and design processes. On February 28 and March 1, a bevy of additional files were posted, along with a number of pro-Ukraine tweets. Among both sets of leaked messages, there were a number of usernames and passwords for a variety of accounts. Additionally, user @ContiLeaks shared access details for a number of alleged Conti command and control servers, plus storage servers for stolen files. However, we have not accessed any of the data necessitating access to remote servers or the use of usernames and passwords, and we strongly recommend against doing so. @ContiLeaks also shared a file that they purport to be the source code for the Conti ransomware but declined to share the password except with “trusted parties.” @ContiLeaks did, however, name one alleged Conti developer, providing their email address and Github. The scale of the leaked information suggests that the leaker is likely either a very senior member of the group or a coalition of disgruntled Conti affiliates. Conti is a business – and a well-funded one Much of the discussion within the chat logs concerns fairly mundane things – interviewing potential operators of the group, payment for services, out-of-office messages, gossip, and discussions of products. Based on the leaked chats, the Conti interview process actually looks a lot like a standard technical interview, with coding exercises to be performed hosted on public code repositories, salary negotiations, and the status of ongoing products. In addition to other financial information related to specific actors, the leaked chats have revealed Conti’s primary Bitcoin address, which contains over two billion USD as of February 28, 2022. Moreover, a conversation on April 9, 2021 between “mango” and “johnyboy77” indicates Russian FSB involvement in some portion of their funding and that the FSB were interested in files from the media outlet Bellingcat on “Navalny” – an apparent reference to Alexei Navalny, the currently imprisoned opposition leader in Russia. Conti development Conti seems to operate much like a software company – the chat logs disclose concerns with the development of specific features for targets and a particular difficulty in encrypting very large files. The Conti team also attempted to get demos of popular endpoint detection software with the intent to develop their malware to avoid detection. Two of the actors, “lemur” and “terry” shared phishing templates (included verbatim in Appendix B at the end of this post) to be used against potential targets. Conti gains initial access in many ways, with phishing a popular line of attack due in part to its relatively high efficacy and low cost. Conti often uses phishing emails to establish a presence on targeted networks. A screenshot of the Conti control panel was also leaked, showing a number of compromised hosts and a breakdown of the operating systems, antiviruses, user rights, and detailed information about the infected assets. Further discussions detailed the use of infrastructure against targets, disclosing a number of both known and unknown Conti command and control domains. At the time of this post, only a small number of the previously unknown command and control domains appear to be active. Conversations between two operators, “Stern” and “Bentley” discuss the use of third parties for malicious documents, favoring certain providers over others. They also discuss logistics for how to deliver ransomware without being detected by dynamic analysis. In a conversation between the two back in June of 2021, Stern discloses that Conti wants to start their own cryptocurrency but does not know who to work with. There is no evidence that anything came of this desire, and Conti continues to use Bitcoin for their ransoms. Other groups assert they are strictly business In stark contrast to Conti, other groups have made it clear to the public that despite their “business model,” they take no public stance on this crisis. LockBit is remaining aloof from the conflict and made it clear that they intend to operate as usual. Although it is believed that LockBit is a Russian organization, they assert that “we are all simple and peaceful people, we are all Earthlings,” and “for us it is just business and we are all apolitical.” Another ransomware group, ALPHV, claims to be “extremely saddened” by Conti’s pledge of support and condemns Conti. Their message concludes, “The Internet, and even more so its dark side, is not the place for politics.” Rumors of Conti’s demise have been greatly exaggerated Conti’s payment and “support” portal is still live, even following the infighting and leaks. Conti has repeatedly proven to be one of the most capable ransomware actors and these chats indicate that the group is well-organized and still very well-funded despite the schism. Any suggestion that these leaks spell the end for Conti is overstated, and we expect that Conti will continue to be a powerful player in the ransomware space. What you can do We are keeping an eye on dark web activity related to Conti and other ransomware groups and want to reiterate the following steps for protecting yourself from ransomware: User education, especially related to well-crafted phishing campaigns Asset and vulnerability management, including reducing your external attack surface Multi-factor authentication Additionally, it is worth ensuring that you are well-guarded against the exploits and malware commonly used by Conti (vulnerabilities provided in Appendix A at the end of this post). Furthermore, security teams should also take some time to review CISA’s recent report on the group. For further discussion on how to protect yourself from ransomware, see our ransomware prevention solution . Verizon's DBIR reported that 2021-2022 saw a 13% increase, approximately the same level of growth observed in the last five years combined. Verizon's researchers took a closer look at this trend and unearthed some useful context. First, they found that ransomware had been present in about 70% of malware breaches over the previous year. Approximately two in five ransomware incidents used desktop sharing software and involved a confidentiality compromise with respect to the CIA Triad . Slightly fewer (35%) leveraged email as an attack vector. What's Behind The Rise in Ransomware? An important cause of ransomware's growth is the shift towards commercialization of cybercrime. Indeed, many of the most prolific cybercriminal groups have undergone significant changes in operations to scale efforts and expand revenue. In several instances, public reporting has shown these groups incorporating divisions previously associated with legitimate corporations including HR departments with recruiters, finance and accounting, as well as negotiators to coordinate ransom payment. Beyond these structures, likely the most significant trend has been the shift to Ransomware as a Service (RaaS), which has seen groups lease out malware to affiliates who conduct intrusions and share profits with the developers (often in a 70-30 split). The below graphic depicts the RaaS relationship and the part that initial access brokers (IABs) play in greater detail. Source: Alan Liska, Ransomware: Understand. Prevent. Recover. Several sources of evidence point to cybercrime's growing commercialization but none as explicitly as the recent Conti leaks. Let’s examine what insights it offered below. Overview of Conti RaaS Conti was a notorious RaaS operation that used double extortion to pressure victims into paying up. It also appears to have had ties to other malware outfits, most notably TrickBot . Conti ransom note template (Source: Bleeping Computer ) Following Russia's invasion of Ukraine on February 24, 2022, the Conti operators announced their "full support" for Russia. Just a few days following this commitment, a Twitter account dubbed " Contileaks " dumped an archive of chat messages taken from Conti's internal communications dating back to the beginning of 2021, as reported by KrebsonSecurity . It also published additional internal chats from 2020. In the months that followed, Conti's handlers began dismantling their operations. In May 2022 , Bleeping Computer wrote that the larger Conti platform had shut down and rebranded into several smaller units, gaining even greater mobility (and evasion from law enforcement) for its members. It was about a month after that when the RaaS operation shut down its data leaks and negotiation infrastructure. Findings of the Conti Leaks The Conti leaks have provided several important insights into how a major RaaS group carries out its operations. These include how Conti ran its "office" and how it worked to improve its "product." Distinct Employees with Distinct Goals In the second part of his investigation on the Conti leaks, KrebsonSecurity revealed that Conti's handlers divided their operations into several business units and brought on staff with specific skill sets. For example, it hired programmers as "Coders" to write malicious code and integrate different technologies, while it relied on "Testers" to validate how the ransomware payload performed against security technologies. The operation also had "Administrators," "Reverse Engineers," and "Penetration Testers/Hackers" working internally, with spamming functions contracted outside the organization. Each of those departments had its own budget, though business units were able to borrow funds from one another. According to a Conti insider, the gang employed more than 60 people – mostly Coders and Testers – in July 2021. That number didn't remain consistent, however, as the group sometimes let people go following internal security breaches. Streamlined Operations to Improve Their 'Product' The third installment of KrebsonSecurity's analysis revealed that the Conti gang took several steps to improve its "product" on an ongoing basis. These initiatives included the following: Allocating $60,000 to acquire a valid license for the Cobalt Strike network penetration testing and reconnaissance tool. Budgeting several thousand dollars each month to pay for security and antivirus software that the "Testers" could use for their evaluations. Redefining the focus of the "Reverse Engineers" in July 2021 to concentrate on Windows 11, Microsoft's newest operating system at the time. The MS-ISAC Perspective on the Conti Leaks To get more insight into the Conti leaks, we sat down with the Cyber Threat Intelligence (CTI) team at the Multi-State Information Sharing and Analysis Center (MS-ISAC). Here's what they had to say. How does commercialization help malicious actors like Conti's operators? Organized ransomware groups operating in a corporate structure allow cybercriminals to conduct highly impactful attacks at scale. For example, instead of expending time and resources on gaining initial access to a victim’s environment, a ransomware group can outsource this work by purchasing already established access from IABs. As a result, ransomware affiliates tasked with conducting attacks are able to increase their number of victims, creating a more dangerous cyber threat landscape for network defenders. Operating through affiliates offers several benefits to the RaaS operator. Principally, because they're not conducting intrusions themselves, they're able to offload risk and dramatically increase the number of potential targets, as there's theoretically no limit to the number of affiliates who can carry out these intrusions. This allows the developers to focus efforts and capital on developing and retooling their software, thereby reinvesting in the enterprise. Has the MS-ISAC seen evidence of cybercrime's commercialization in the daily work of supporting members? If so, what has this looked like? Yes, the MS-ISAC regularly receives reporting about SLTT ransomware attacks involving sophisticated RaaS groups like Conti. From mid-2020 through January 2022, for instance, 22 Conti-related SLTT ransomware attacks were reported to the MS-ISAC, impacting organizations ranging from municipal governments to education facilities. Open-source reporting indicates that the “Conti group” is also tied to the Ryuk ransomware variant, which impacted an additional 89 SLTT government entities from late 2018 through mid-2021. To this day, other RaaS groups continue to attack SLTT governments, including at least 23 ransomware attacks associated with the LockBit 2.0 variant since August 2021. Where does cybercrime's commercialization put an emphasis for the future? I would say it only increases the victim set. Ultimately, there's no silver bullet against ransomware. But SLTTs can still do their best to have their bases covered and put themselves in the best position to prevent and react to breaches when they occur. That means becoming members of the MS-ISAC so they can receive our products, leverage our resources, and deploy appropriate protections. For our team, we need to watch closely for shifts in tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs) that could catch members by surprise, and we need to provide the timely intelligence and guidance that will help them proactively defend their networks. If threat actors evolve, we need to, as well. This also includes things like bolstering partnerships that allow us to share timely intel with members. The Center for Internet Security and the MS-ISAC understand the formidable threat RaaS groups present to SLTTs. They offer services and resources to help organizations better defend themselves. These include no-cost services like Malicious Domain Blocking and Reporting (MDBR), which prevents IT systems from connecting to harmful web domains and thereby helps to limit infections related to known malware, ransomware, phishing, and other cyber threats. A robust ransomware defense should also involve some form of endpoint security solution such as the CIS Endpoint Security Services (ESS), which is available to SLTTs through a partnership with CrowdStrike. Finally, the threat underscores the importance for SLTTs to implement the cybersecurity best practices found in the CIS Critical Security Controls , which are designed to prevent all types of cyber attacks. Defending Against Ransomware Like Conti The CTI team's thoughts on the Conti leaks point to an important truth about ransomware. Certainly, some attackers have taken it upon themselves in recent years to restructure as RaaS operations and commercialize their business functions. But for all its innovations, ransomware's aims have not fundamentally changed as a threat. Its purpose still revolves around denying access to files by encrypting infected machines. Subsequently, MS-ISAC members can use the solutions identified by the CTI team along with these resources to strengthen their defenses against ransomware going forward. Malicious cyber actors known by their online aliases of “Target,” “Reshaev,” “Professor,” “Tramp,” and “Dandis” are believed to be linked to the Conti ransomware group. Conti (also known as Wizard Spider), is a Russian government-linked ransomware-as-a-service (RaaS) group that has targeted U.S. and Western critical infrastructure. After Russian military forces invaded neighboring Ukraine in February 2022, Conti ransomware operators pledged support to the Russian government and threatened critical infrastructure organizations of countries perceived to carry out cyberattacks or war against the Russian government. First detected in 2019, Conti ransomware has been used to conduct more than 1,000 ransomware operations targeting U.S. and international critical infrastructure, such as law enforcement agencies, emergency medical services, 9-1-1 dispatch centers, and municipalities. These healthcare and first responder networks are among the more than 400 organizations worldwide victimized by Conti, over 290 of which are located in the United States. Conti operators typically steal victims’ files and encrypt the servers and workstations in an effort to force a ransom payment from the victim. The ransom letter instructs victims to contact the actors through an online portal to complete the transaction. If the ransom is not paid, the stolen data is sold or published to a public site controlled by the Conti actors. Ransom amounts vary widely, with some ransom demands being as high as $25 million. At that time, we assessed that due to their sophisticated capability, deep funding, and quick recovery from exposed infrastructure in November 2021, they remained an active and significant threat. As of March 9, 2022, our threat intelligence team has observed a resumption of normal operations from Conti. On February 27, Twitter user @ContiLeaks released a trove of chat logs from the ransomware group, Conti – a sophisticated ransomware group whose manual was publicly leaked last year . Ahead of the chat log disclosures, Conti pledged their support for the Russian Government following the Russian invasion of Ukraine. However, a number of members sided with Ukraine, causing strife within the organization. Two days later, Conti posted a second message revising their statement to condemn the war and to strike back only if Russian critical infrastructure is targeted. At the time of the leak, a file titled `1.tgz` was released on the “AnonFiles” website, containing 14 megabytes of chat logs across 393 JSON files. However, some of the messages were encrypted and could not be read, so the information provided is necessarily incomplete. The remaining files contained internal Conti communications, screenshots of tools, and discussions of their exploits and design processes. On February 28 and March 1, a bevy of additional files were posted, along with a number of pro-Ukraine tweets. Among both sets of leaked messages, there were a number of usernames and passwords for a variety of accounts. Additionally, user @ContiLeaks shared access details for a number of alleged Conti command and control servers, plus storage servers for stolen files. However, we have not accessed any of the data necessitating access to remote servers or the use of usernames and passwords, and we strongly recommend against doing so. @ContiLeaks also shared a file that they purport to be the source code for the Conti ransomware but declined to share the password except with “trusted parties.” @ContiLeaks did, however, name one alleged Conti developer, providing their email address and Github. The scale of the leaked information suggests that the leaker is likely either a very senior member of the group or a coalition of disgruntled Conti affiliates. Conti is a business – and a well-funded one Much of the discussion within the chat logs concerns fairly mundane things – interviewing potential operators of the group, payment for services, out-of-office messages, gossip, and discussions of products. Based on the leaked chats, the Conti interview process actually looks a lot like a standard technical interview, with coding exercises to be performed hosted on public code repositories, salary negotiations, and the status of ongoing products. In addition to other financial information related to specific actors, the leaked chats have revealed Conti’s primary Bitcoin address, which contains over two billion USD as of February 28, 2022. Moreover, a conversation on April 9, 2021 between “mango” and “johnyboy77” indicates Russian FSB involvement in some portion of their funding and that the FSB were interested in files from the media outlet Bellingcat on “Navalny” – an apparent reference to Alexei Navalny, the currently imprisoned opposition leader in Russia. Conti development Conti seems to operate much like a software company – the chat logs disclose concerns with the development of specific features for targets and a particular difficulty in encrypting very large files. The Conti team also attempted to get demos of popular endpoint detection software with the intent to develop their malware to avoid detection. Two of the actors, “lemur” and “terry” shared phishing templates (included verbatim in Appendix B at the end of this post) to be used against potential targets. Conti gains initial access in many ways, with phishing a popular line of attack due in part to its relatively high efficacy and low cost. Conti often uses phishing emails to establish a presence on targeted networks. A screenshot of the Conti control panel was also leaked, showing a number of compromised hosts and a breakdown of the operating systems, antiviruses, user rights, and detailed information about the infected assets. Further discussions detailed the use of infrastructure against targets, disclosing a number of both known and unknown Conti command and control domains. At the time of this post, only a small number of the previously unknown command and control domains appear to be active. Conversations between two operators, “Stern” and “Bentley” discuss the use of third parties for malicious documents, favoring certain providers over others. They also discuss logistics for how to deliver ransomware without being detected by dynamic analysis. In a conversation between the two back in June of 2021, Stern discloses that Conti wants to start their own cryptocurrency but does not know who to work with. There is no evidence that anything came of this desire, and Conti continues to use Bitcoin for their ransoms. Other groups assert they are strictly business In stark contrast to Conti, other groups have made it clear to the public that despite their “business model,” they take no public stance on this crisis. LockBit is remaining aloof from the conflict and made it clear that they intend to operate as usual. Although it is believed that LockBit is a Russian organization, they assert that “we are all simple and peaceful people, we are all Earthlings,” and “for us it is just business and we are all apolitical.” Another ransomware group, ALPHV, claims to be “extremely saddened” by Conti’s pledge of support and condemns Conti. Their message concludes, “The Internet, and even more so its dark side, is not the place for politics.” Rumors of Conti’s demise have been greatly exaggerated Conti’s payment and “support” portal is still live, even following the infighting and leaks. Conti has repeatedly proven to be one of the most capable ransomware actors and these chats indicate that the group is well-organized and still very well-funded despite the schism. Any suggestion that these leaks spell the end for Conti is overstated, and we expect that Conti will continue to be a powerful player in the ransomware space. What you can do We are keeping an eye on dark web activity related to Conti and other ransomware groups and want to reiterate the following steps for protecting yourself from ransomware: User education, especially related to well-crafted phishing campaigns Asset and vulnerability management, including reducing your external attack surface Multi-factor authentication Additionally, it is worth ensuring that you are well-guarded against the exploits and malware commonly used by Conti (vulnerabilities provided in Appendix A at the end of this post). Furthermore, security teams should also take some time to review CISA’s recent report on the group. Verizon's DBIR reported that 2021-2022 saw a 13% increase, approximately the same level of growth observed in the last five years combined. Verizon's researchers took a closer look at this trend and unearthed some useful context. First, they found that ransomware had been present in about 70% of malware breaches over the previous year. Approximately two in five ransomware incidents used desktop sharing software and involved a confidentiality compromise with respect to the CIA Triad . Slightly fewer (35%) leveraged email as an attack vector. What's Behind The Rise in Ransomware? An important cause of ransomware's growth is the shift towards commercialization of cybercrime. Indeed, many of the most prolific cybercriminal groups have undergone significant changes in operations to scale efforts and expand revenue. In several instances, public reporting has shown these groups incorporating divisions previously associated with legitimate corporations including HR departments with recruiters, finance and accounting, as well as negotiators to coordinate ransom payment. Beyond these structures, likely the most significant trend has been the shift to Ransomware as a Service (RaaS), which has seen groups lease out malware to affiliates who conduct intrusions and share profits with the developers (often in a 70-30 split). The below graphic depicts the RaaS relationship and the part that initial access brokers (IABs) play in greater detail. Source: Alan Liska, Ransomware: Understand. Prevent. Recover. Several sources of evidence point to cybercrime's growing commercialization but none as explicitly as the recent Conti leaks. Let’s examine what insights it offered below. Overview of Conti RaaS Conti was a notorious RaaS operation that used double extortion to pressure victims into paying up. It also appears to have had ties to other malware outfits, most notably TrickBot . Conti ransom note template (Source: Bleeping Computer ) Following Russia's invasion of Ukraine on February 24, 2022, the Conti operators announced their "full support" for Russia. Just a few days following this commitment, a Twitter account dubbed " Contileaks " dumped an archive of chat messages taken from Conti's internal communications dating back to the beginning of 2021, as reported by KrebsonSecurity . It also published additional internal chats from 2020. In the months that followed, Conti's handlers began dismantling their operations. In May 2022 , Bleeping Computer wrote that the larger Conti platform had shut down and rebranded into several smaller units, gaining even greater mobility (and evasion from law enforcement) for its members. It was about a month after that when the RaaS operation shut down its data leaks and negotiation infrastructure. Findings of the Conti Leaks The Conti leaks have provided several important insights into how a major RaaS group carries out its operations. These include how Conti ran its "office" and how it worked to improve its "product." Distinct Employees with Distinct Goals In the second part of his investigation on the Conti leaks, KrebsonSecurity revealed that Conti's handlers divided their operations into several business units and brought on staff with specific skill sets. For example, it hired programmers as "Coders" to write malicious code and integrate different technologies, while it relied on "Testers" to validate how the ransomware payload performed against security technologies. The operation also had "Administrators," "Reverse Engineers," and "Penetration Testers/Hackers" working internally, with spamming functions contracted outside the organization. Each of those departments had its own budget, though business units were able to borrow funds from one another. According to a Conti insider, the gang employed more than 60 people – mostly Coders and Testers – in July 2021. That number didn't remain consistent, however, as the group sometimes let people go following internal security breaches. Streamlined Operations to Improve Their 'Product' The third installment of KrebsonSecurity's analysis revealed that the Conti gang took several steps to improve its "product" on an ongoing basis. These initiatives included the following: Allocating $60,000 to acquire a valid license for the Cobalt Strike network penetration testing and reconnaissance tool. Budgeting several thousand dollars each month to pay for security and antivirus software that the "Testers" could use for their evaluations. Redefining the focus of the "Reverse Engineers" in July 2021 to concentrate on Windows 11, Microsoft's newest operating system at the time. The MS-ISAC Perspective on the Conti Leaks To get more insight into the Conti leaks, we sat down with the Cyber Threat Intelligence (CTI) team at the Multi-State Information Sharing and Analysis Center (MS-ISAC). Here's what they had to say. How does commercialization help malicious actors like Conti's operators? Organized ransomware groups operating in a corporate structure allow cybercriminals to conduct highly impactful attacks at scale. For example, instead of expending time and resources on gaining initial access to a victim’s environment, a ransomware group can outsource this work by purchasing already established access from IABs. As a result, ransomware affiliates tasked with conducting attacks are able to increase their number of victims, creating a more dangerous cyber threat landscape for network defenders. Operating through affiliates offers several benefits to the RaaS operator. Principally, because they're not conducting intrusions themselves, they're able to offload risk and dramatically increase the number of potential targets, as there's theoretically no limit to the number of affiliates who can carry out these intrusions. This allows the developers to focus efforts and capital on developing and retooling their software, thereby reinvesting in the enterprise. Has the MS-ISAC seen evidence of cybercrime's commercialization in the daily work of supporting members? If so, what has this looked like? Yes, the MS-ISAC regularly receives reporting about SLTT ransomware attacks involving sophisticated RaaS groups like Conti. From mid-2020 through January 2022, for instance, 22 Conti-related SLTT ransomware attacks were reported to the MS-ISAC, impacting organizations ranging from municipal governments to education facilities. Open-source reporting indicates that the “Conti group” is also tied to the Ryuk ransomware variant, which impacted an additional 89 SLTT government entities from late 2018 through mid-2021. To this day, other RaaS groups continue to attack SLTT governments, including at least 23 ransomware attacks associated with the LockBit 2.0 variant since August 2021. Where does cybercrime's commercialization put an emphasis for the future? I would say it only increases the victim set. Ultimately, there's no silver bullet against ransomware. But SLTTs can still do their best to have their bases covered and put themselves in the best position to prevent and react to breaches when they occur. That means becoming members of the MS-ISAC so they can receive our products, leverage our resources, and deploy appropriate protections. For our team, we need to watch closely for shifts in tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs) that could catch members by surprise, and we need to provide the timely intelligence and guidance that will help them proactively defend their networks. If threat actors evolve, we need to, as well. This also includes things like bolstering partnerships that allow us to share timely intel with members. The Center for Internet Security and the MS-ISAC understand the formidable threat RaaS groups present to SLTTs. They offer services and resources to help organizations better defend themselves. These include no-cost services like Malicious Domain Blocking and Reporting (MDBR), which prevents IT systems from connecting to harmful web domains and thereby helps to limit infections related to known malware, ransomware, phishing, and other cyber threats. A robust ransomware defense should also involve some form of endpoint security solution such as the CIS Endpoint Security Services (ESS), which is available to SLTTs through a partnership with CrowdStrike. Finally, the threat underscores the importance for SLTTs to implement the cybersecurity best practices found in the CIS Critical Security Controls , which are designed to prevent all types of cyber attacks. Defending Against Ransomware Like Conti The CTI team's thoughts on the Conti leaks point to an important truth about ransomware. Certainly, some attackers have taken it upon themselves in recent years to restructure as RaaS operations and commercialize their business functions. But for all its innovations, ransomware's aims have not fundamentally changed as a threat. Its purpose still revolves around denying access to files by encrypting infected machines. Subsequently, MS-ISAC members can use the solutions identified by the CTI team along with these resources to strengthen their defenses against ransomware going forward.
